claims.source: Here, we investigated the role of the CCP1 domain of the HpARI proteins, and found that HpARI1 and HpARI2 can also bind to heparan sulphate (HS) via their CCP1 domain, while HpARI3 cannot.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by multiple binding assays shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Extracellular matrix binding extends the half-life of HpARI2 in vivo at the site of administration.
claims.source: This extracellular matrix binding extends the half-life of HpARI2 in vivo at the site of administration.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing HpARI2 retains activity when administered 3 days prior to allergen, while mutants lacking HS binding do not (Figures 3, 6).

claims.claim: HpARI2 suppresses the release of IL-33 measured by western blot due to its tethering function.
claims.source: As shown previously, HpARI2 suppressed the release of IL-33 measured by western blot, due to its tethering function (Osbourn et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C and supported by cited study (Osbourn et al., 2017).

claims.claim: HpARI1 showed a trend toward suppressing IL-33 release that did not reach statistical significance.
claims.source: HpARI1 showed a similar trend which did not reach statistical significance in this experiment.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: HpARI3 does not alter the levels of released IL-33 as assessed by western blot.
claims.source: HpARI3 lacked this ability and did not alter the levels of released IL-33 as assessed by western blot.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: HpARI1 only binds 50% of DNA in EMSA assays.
claims.source: Interestingly, while HpARI2 effectively bound all DNA, HpARI1 showed a reduced DNA-binding ability, only binding 50% of the DNA in this assay (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Quantified from EMSA data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The DNA-binding activity of HpARI2 is localized to its CCP1 domain.
claims.source: The DNA-binding activity of HpARI2 was previously shown to be localised to its CCP1 domain.
claims.evidence: Supported by previous work (Osbourn et al., 2017) and confirmed by domain-swap experiments in Figure 1F-G.

claims.claim: HpARI fusion proteins show DNA binding directly related to the source of their CCP1 domain.
claims.source: In EMSA experiments, these constructs showed DNA binding directly related to the source of their CCP1 domain, with HpARI3:2 lacking, and HpARI2:3 showing DNA binding (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Members of the HpARI family differ in their ability to bind both IL-33 and DNA.
claims.source: Therefore, members of the HpARI family differ in their ability to bind both IL-33 and DNA, the latter of which is mediated solely by the CCP1 domain.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: DNA binding by HpARI proteins is mediated solely by the CCP1 domain.
claims.source: Therefore, members of the HpARI family differ in their ability to bind both IL-33 and DNA, the latter of which is mediated solely by the CCP1 domain.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by domain-swap experiments shown in Figure 1F-G.

claims.claim: HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins represent useful tools to separate the DNA binding and IL-33 modulation effects.
claims.source: The HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins represent useful tools to separate the DNA binding and IL-33 modulation effects of HpARI2 and HpARI3, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the design of the fusion proteins shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: HpARI2 dose-dependently suppresses ILC2 responses in vitro.
claims.source: As shown previously (Colomb et al., 2024), in this assay HpARI2 dose-dependently suppresses ILC2 responses, while HpARI3 amplifies them (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A and supported by cited study (Colomb et al., 2024).

claims.claim: HpARI3 amplifies ILC2 responses in vitro.
claims.source: As shown previously (Colomb et al., 2024), in this assay HpARI2 dose-dependently suppresses ILC2 responses, while HpARI3 amplifies them (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A and supported by cited study (Colomb et al., 2024).

claims.claim: HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins retain the amplifying or suppressing activities of their CCP2/3 domains.
claims.source: The HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins retained the amplifying or suppressing activities of their CCP2/3 domains.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A showing HpARI2:3 amplifies and HpARI3:2 suppresses ILC2 responses.

claims.claim: HpARI2:3 shows decreased activity compared to HpARI3 wild-type (HpARI3 EC50=1.2 ng/ml, HpARI2:3 EC50=21.5 ng/ml).
claims.source: Small alterations in activity were seen when CCP1 domains were swapped, with HpARI2:3 showing decreased activity compared to HpARI3 wild-type (HpARI3 EC50=1.2 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 EC50=21.5 ng/ml), and HpARI3:2 showing slightly increased activity compared to HpARI2 wild-type (HpARI2 IC50=1.9 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 IC50=1.1 ng/ml).
claims.evidence: Calculated from dose-response curves shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: HpARI3:2 shows slightly increased activity compared to HpARI2 wild-type (HpARI2 IC50=1.9 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 IC50=1.1 ng/ml).
claims.source: Small alterations in activity were seen when CCP1 domains were swapped, with HpARI2:3 showing decreased activity compared to HpARI3 wild-type (HpARI3 EC50=1.2 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 EC50=21.5 ng/ml), and HpARI3:2 showing slightly increased activity compared to HpARI2 wild-type (HpARI2 IC50=1.9 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 IC50=1.1 ng/ml).
claims.evidence: Calculated from dose-response curves shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: HpARI2 and HpARI2:3 tether IL-33 and reduce its release when co-administered with Alternaria allergen.
claims.source: As expected, HpARI2 and HpARI2:3 tethered IL-33 and reduced its release, due to their combination of IL-33 and DNA-binding activities.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: HpARI3 and HpARI3:2 slightly increase levels of IL-33 in BAL, possibly due to binding and stabilization of the soluble cytokine.
claims.source: HpARI3 and HpARI3:2 lack tethering ability, and slightly increased levels of IL-33 in BAL, possibly due to binding and stabilisation of the soluble cytokine in the absence of DNA binding (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Observed in western blot data shown in Figure 2B, with speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: IL-33 tethering does not correlate with suppression of IL-33-induced responses at 24 hours.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, when the downstream response to released IL-33 was measured 24 hr later (Figure 2C), IL-33 tethering did not correlate with suppression of IL-33-induced responses: while HpARI2 suppressed and HpARI3 amplified eosinophilia, ILC2 activation (as measured by surface CD25 or cell size by median FSC), and IL-5 release (Figure 2D–H), HpARI2:3 could not suppress IL-33 responses despite tethering of IL-33 at the 15 min timepoint (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by comparing IL-33 tethering at 15 min (Figure 2B) with downstream responses at 24 hr (Figure 2D-H).

claims.claim: HpARI2:3 amplifies IL-33-dependent responses similarly to HpARI3 despite tethering IL-33.
claims.source: In fact, HpARI2:3 amplified IL-33-dependent responses similarly to HpARI3, and tended to have increased activity compared to the HpARI3 wild-type protein.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2D-H showing HpARI2:3 amplifies eosinophilia, ILC2 activation, and IL-5 release.

claims.claim: HpARI3:2 is capable of effectively blocking IL-33-dependent responses despite lacking IL-33 tethering.
claims.source: Similarly, despite a lack of IL-33 tethering, HpARI3:2 was capable of effectively blocking IL-33-dependent responses similarly to HpARI2 wild-type protein (Figure 2D–H).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2D-H showing HpARI3:2 suppresses eosinophilia, ILC2 activation, and IL-5 release.

claims.claim: The model of DNA tethering of IL-33 by HpARI2 cannot fully explain the activity of these proteins.
claims.source: Therefore, these data indicated that our model of DNA tethering of IL-33 by HpARI2 could not fully explain the activity of these proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the unexpected results shown in Figure 2 where tethering did not correlate with suppression.

claims.claim: The altered activity of the fusion proteins could be due to their effective half-life in vivo.
claims.source: We hypothesised that the altered activity of the fusion proteins could be due to their effective half-life in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the unexpected results, tested in subsequent experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: HpARI2 can suppress Alternaria-induced eosinophilia and ILC2 responses when administered 3 days prior to allergen.
claims.source: We administered HpARI2 or HpARI3:2 either 1 day, 3 days, or 7 days prior to Alternaria (Figure 3A), and found that while HpARI2 could suppress Alternaria-induced eosinophilia and ILC2 responses when administered 3 days prior to allergen, HpARI3:2 could only replicate this suppression when administered 24 hr prior to Alternaria (Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3B-E showing HpARI2 retains activity at day -3.

claims.claim: HpARI3:2 can only suppress Alternaria-induced responses when administered 24 hr prior to allergen.
claims.source: We administered HpARI2 or HpARI3:2 either 1 day, 3 days, or 7 days prior to Alternaria (Figure 3A), and found that while HpARI2 could suppress Alternaria-induced eosinophilia and ILC2 responses when administered 3 days prior to allergen, HpARI3:2 could only replicate this suppression when administered 24 hr prior to Alternaria (Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3B-E showing HpARI3:2 loses activity at day -3.

claims.claim: The in vivo half-life of HpARI2 is controlled by the CCP1 domain.
claims.source: Therefore, the in vivo half-life of HpARI2 is controlled by the CCP1 domain, and the HpARI3 CCP1 domain confers a shorter in vivo half-life than the HpARI2 counterpart.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 3 showing HpARI3:2 (with HpARI3 CCP1) has shorter activity than HpARI2.

claims.claim: The HpARI3 CCP1 domain confers a shorter in vivo half-life than the HpARI2 CCP1 domain.
claims.source: Therefore, the in vivo half-life of HpARI2 is controlled by the CCP1 domain, and the HpARI3 CCP1 domain confers a shorter in vivo half-life than the HpARI2 counterpart.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 3 showing HpARI3:2 has shorter activity than HpARI2.

claims.claim: Extracellular DNA is present at very low concentrations in bronchoalveolar lavage at homeostasis.
claims.source: As extracellular DNA is only present in the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) at very low concentrations at homeostasis (Curren et al., 2023), and is released in response to stimuli such as Alternaria, we hypothesised that the HpARI2 CCP1 could have a second binding partner which mediates its long in vivo half-life.
claims.evidence: Supported by cited study (Curren et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Extracellular DNA is released in response to stimuli such as Alternaria.
claims.source: As extracellular DNA is only present in the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) at very low concentrations at homeostasis (Curren et al., 2023), and is released in response to stimuli such as Alternaria, we hypothesised that the HpARI2 CCP1 could have a second binding partner which mediates its long in vivo half-life.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Alternaria-induced responses.

claims.claim: Other host and pathogen CCP domain proteins interact with extracellular matrix constituents such as HS.
claims.source: As other host and pathogen CCP domain proteins have been demonstrated to interact with extracellular matrix constituents such as HS (Mark et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2008), we hypothesised that this could be the case for the HpARIs also.
claims.evidence: Supported by cited studies (Mark et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2008).

claims.claim: HS addition results in earlier elution of HpARI1 and HpARI2 in gel filtration chromatography.
claims.source: We first used gel filtration chromatography to assess the mobility of HpARIs in the presence or absence of HS. While HS addition resulted in earlier elution of HpARI1 and HpARI2, no shift was seen with HpARI3, implying a lack of HS binding (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: No shift in gel filtration elution is seen with HpARI3 upon HS addition, implying a lack of HS binding.
claims.source: We first used gel filtration chromatography to assess the mobility of HpARIs in the presence or absence of HS. While HS addition resulted in earlier elution of HpARI1 and HpARI2, no shift was seen with HpARI3, implying a lack of HS binding (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 can be pulled down with heparin-coated beads.
claims.source: Likewise, HpARI1 and HpARI2 could be pulled down with heparin-coated beads while HpARI3 could not (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by heparin-agarose pull-down assays shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: HpARI3 cannot be pulled down with heparin-coated beads.
claims.source: Likewise, HpARI1 and HpARI2 could be pulled down with heparin-coated beads while HpARI3 could not (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by heparin-agarose pull-down assays shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: HS is present on cell surface proteoglycans.
claims.source: As well as being a common constituent of the extracellular matrix, HS is present on cell surface proteoglycans (Xu and Esko, 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by cited review (Xu and Esko, 2014).

claims.claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind strongly to CD45-negative stromal cells in mouse lung.
claims.source: To assess whether HS binding could mediate interactions between the HpARIs and stromal cells, we added PE-conjugated tetramers of the HpARIs to preparations of naïve mouse lung cells, showing that HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind strongly to CD45-negative stromal cells, but less to CD45-positive cells, while HpARI3 did not show detectable binding to any lung cells (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry cell-binding assays shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind less to CD45-positive cells than to CD45-negative cells.
claims.source: To assess whether HS binding could mediate interactions between the HpARIs and stromal cells, we added PE-conjugated tetramers of the HpARIs to preparations of naïve mouse lung cells, showing that HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind strongly to CD45-negative stromal cells, but less to CD45-positive cells, while HpARI3 did not show detectable binding to any lung cells (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry cell-binding assays shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: HpARI3 does not show detectable binding to any lung cells.
claims.source: To assess whether HS binding could mediate interactions between the HpARIs and stromal cells, we added PE-conjugated tetramers of the HpARIs to preparations of naïve mouse lung cells, showing that HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind strongly to CD45-negative stromal cells, but less to CD45-positive cells, while HpARI3 did not show detectable binding to any lung cells (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry cell-binding assays shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: HpARI1 has an affinity for HS of 9.6 μM.
claims.source: Finally, to assess the respective affinities for HS, we used isothermal calorimetry to show that HpARI1 had an affinity for HS of 9.6 μM, while HpARI2 had a slightly higher affinity of 4.2 μM.
claims.evidence: Measured by isothermal calorimetry shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: HpARI2 has an affinity for HS of 4.2 μM.
claims.source: Finally, to assess the respective affinities for HS, we used isothermal calorimetry to show that HpARI1 had an affinity for HS of 9.6 μM, while HpARI2 had a slightly higher affinity of 4.2 μM.
claims.evidence: Measured by isothermal calorimetry shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: No binding could be detected between HpARI3 and HS by isothermal calorimetry.
claims.source: Furthermore, these experiments confirmed that no binding could be detected between HpARI3 and HS (Figure 4D–F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by isothermal calorimetry shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 contain a strongly positively charged surface in their CCP1 domains.
claims.source: We next used protein modelling to understand the differential HS binding of different HpARIs. AlphaFold2 models were produced to predict the structures of the CCP1 domains of HpARI1, HpARI2, and HpARI3. This revealed that while HpARI1 and HpARI2 contain a strongly positively charged surface, HpARI3 lacks this charged surface (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by AlphaFold2 modeling and electrostatic surface analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: HpARI3 lacks a positively charged surface in its CCP1 domain.
claims.source: We next used protein modelling to understand the differential HS binding of different HpARIs. AlphaFold2 models were produced to predict the structures of the CCP1 domains of HpARI1, HpARI2, and HpARI3. This revealed that while HpARI1 and HpARI2 contain a strongly positively charged surface, HpARI3 lacks this charged surface (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by AlphaFold2 modeling and electrostatic surface analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: HS molecules can dock to various locations across the positively charged surfaces of HpARI1 and HpARI2 CCP1 domains.
claims.source: We next used molecular docking to predict the structure of the complex between HpARI1 or HpARI2 CCP1 domains and the extracellular matrix component HS. Docking experiments predicted that HS molecules can dock to various locations across the positively charged surfaces of HpARI1 and HpARI2 CCP1 domains (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by molecular docking experiments shown in Figure 5B-C.

claims.claim: The CCP1 domain of HpARI1 and HpARI2 has a positively charged surface which acts as a non-specific binding site for negatively charged cellular components, including DNA and HS.
claims.source: Therefore, the CCP1 domain of HpARI1 and -2 has a positively charged surface which acts as a non-specific binding site for negatively charged cellular components, including DNA and HS, but this binding surface is lacking in HpARI3.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling (Figure 5) and binding data (Figures 1, 4).

claims.claim: Five arginine residues in CCP1 of HpARI2 form the positively charged HS- and DNA-binding surface.
claims.source: Electrostatic modelling of HpARI2 indicated that five arginine residues in CCP1 form the positively charged HS- and DNA-binding surface (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Identified by electrostatic modeling shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: HpARI2_pentaR has identical IL-33 suppressive activity in vitro as compared to HpARI2 wild-type.
claims.source: HpARI2_pentaR had identical IL-33 suppressive activity in vitro as compared to HpARI2 wild-type (Figure 6A), indicating its IL-33 binding was unaffected.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro ILC2 assays shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: HpARI2_pentaR lacks binding to heparin.
claims.source: As predicted, however, HpARI2_pentaR lacked binding to both heparin (Figure 6B) and DNA (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by heparin-agarose pull-down assays shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: HpARI2_pentaR lacks binding to DNA.
claims.source: As predicted, however, HpARI2_pentaR lacked binding to both heparin (Figure 6B) and DNA (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: HpARI2_pentaR has a shorter in vivo half-life than wild-type HpARI2.
claims.source: When HpARI2_pentaR was administered to mice prior to Alternaria administration, like HpARI3:2, it was found to have a shorter in vivo half-life than the wild-type HpARI2 protein (Figure 6D–H).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo experiments shown in Figure 6D-H showing loss of activity at day -3.

claims.claim: HpARI2 is an HS-binding protein.
claims.source: Taken together, this data shows that HpARI2 is an HS-binding protein, and that interactions with HS increase its in vivo half-life at the site of administration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the HS-binding data shown in Figures 4-6.

claims.claim: Interactions with HS increase HpARI2's in vivo half-life at the site of administration.
claims.source: Taken together, this data shows that HpARI2 is an HS-binding protein, and that interactions with HS increase its in vivo half-life at the site of administration.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing mutants lacking HS binding have shorter half-lives (Figures 3, 6).

claims.claim: The prototypic Hp-TGM sequence has undergone selection to carry out a range of contradictory functions.
claims.source: Thus the prototypic Hp-TGM sequence has undergone selection to carry out a range of contradictory functions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies showing different Hp-TGM family members have opposing activities.

claims.claim: The activity of the HpARIs is controlled by timing of release, in vivo half-life, and localisation within the host, controlled by interactions with the extracellular matrix.
claims.source: As the Hp-TGM proteins are targeted to different cellular targets through co-receptor interactions, we propose that the activity of the HpARIs is controlled by timing of release, in vivo half-life, and localisation within the host, controlled by interactions with the extracellular matrix.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing HS binding controls half-life.

claims.claim: The positively charged patch in HpARI2's CCP1 domain lengthens the effective half-life of the protein in vivo via binding to DNA and HS.
claims.source: We show here that HpARI1 and HpARI2 have a positively charged patch in their CCP1 domain. In the case of HpARI2, we show that this charged patch lengthens the effective half-life of the protein in vivo via binding to DNA and, more relevantly, HS.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with HpARI2_pentaR mutant lacking the charged patch (Figure 6).

claims.claim: Binding to the extracellular matrix and cell surface proteoglycans prevents diffusion of HpARI1 and HpARI2, keeps the local concentration high, and prevents loss of protein to the circulation.
claims.source: We propose that this binding to the extracellular matrix and cell surface proteoglycans prevents diffusion of HpARI1 and HpARI2, keeps the local concentration high, and prevents loss of protein to the circulation.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data showing HS binding extends half-life.

claims.claim: HpARI2 is a more effective IL-33 suppressor compared to a systemically administered monoclonal antibody due to its extracellular matrix binding.
claims.source: This makes HpARI2 a particularly effective IL-33 suppressor when compared to a systemically administered monoclonal antibody which must reach an effective concentration throughout the circulation of the host to allow blockade at the site of IL-33 release.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative comparison based on the proposed mechanism of HS-mediated localization.

claims.claim: Some cytokines and chemokines bind to the extracellular matrix to ensure their effects are constrained to the local milieu.
claims.source: Some cytokines and chemokines (Ridley et al., 2023) bind to the extracellular matrix to ensure their effects are constrained to the local milieu.
claims.evidence: Supported by cited review (Ridley et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Abrogating the HS-binding activity of IFN-γ results in fatal systemic inflammation after viral infection.
claims.source: This is critical for their activity: it was recently shown that abrogating the HS-binding activity of IFN-γ results in fatal systemic (rather than local) inflammation after viral infection (Kemna et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by cited study (Kemna et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Retaining proteins on the extracellular matrix is being developed for increasing the efficacy of protein-based therapeutics while decreasing toxicity at off-target sites.
claims.source: This approach of retaining proteins on the extracellular matrix is being developed for increasing the efficacy of protein-based therapeutics, while decreasing toxicity at off-target sites (Alshoubaki et al., 2023; Martino et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by cited studies (Alshoubaki et al., 2023; Martino et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Heparin binding prolongs the blocking of VEGF signalling by recombinant VEGFR1 in therapeutic use.
claims.source: This was exemplified in a study showing that heparin binding was able to prolong the blocking of VEGF signalling by recombinant VEGFR1 in therapeutic use (Xin et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by cited study (Xin et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Parasitic helminths have evolved the technique of using extracellular matrix binding to localise immunomodulatory proteins.
claims.source: It appears that this same technique has been evolved by parasitic helminths to localise immunomodulatory proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing HpARI proteins use HS binding for localization.

claims.claim: HS binding has been demonstrated for several other CCP domain proteins, including KCP, Factor H, and C4BP.
claims.source: HS binding has been demonstrated for several other CCP domain proteins, including the viral CCP protein Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus complement control protein (KCP) (Mark et al., 2006), and the mammalian proteins Factor H (Schmidt et al., 2008) and C4BP (Spijkers et al., 2008; Trouw et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by cited studies (Mark et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2008; Spijkers et al., 2008; Trouw et al., 2005).

claims.claim: C4BP presents a basic patch which is able to bind both DNA and HS, similarly to HpARI1 and HpARI2.
claims.source: In C4BP, the protein presents a basic patch which is able to bind both DNA and HS, similarly to the data we show here for HpARI1 and HpARI2.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to established knowledge about C4BP, drawing parallels to the HpARI data.

claims.claim: HpARI1 has lower affinity for DNA and HS compared to HpARI2.
claims.source: While HpARI1 binds to DNA and HS, it has lower affinity for these ligands compared to HpARI2, and in the DNA-binding assays only bound to 50% of the total DNA.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA (Figure 1E) and ITC (Figure 4D-E) showing weaker binding for HpARI1.

claims.claim: HpARI1 may remain partially in solution, diffusing further from the site of deposition than HpARI2.
claims.source: It is unclear what the purpose is of this reduced binding affinity, but it could be that HpARI1 remains partially in solution, diffusing further from the site of deposition than HpARI2, and so mediating its effects at a greater distance from the site of release.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of HpARI1's weaker binding.

claims.claim: IL-33 released by epithelial cells in the intestine induces a type 2 immune response which results in parasite ejection.
claims.source: In parasitic infection, IL-33 released by epithelial cells in the intestine induces a type 2 immune response which results in parasite ejection.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-33's role in anti-parasite immunity.

claims.claim: IL-33 released by myeloid cells in helminth infection induces regulatory T cell expansion, suppressing effector immune responses and resulting in increased parasite burdens.
claims.source: In the same helminth infection model, IL-33 released by myeloid cells induced regulatory T cell expansion, suppressing effector immune responses and resulting in increased parasite burdens (Hung et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by cited study (Hung et al., 2020).

claims.claim: At different sites and in different cells, IL-33 can have directly opposing effects.
claims.source: Therefore, at different sites and in different cells, IL-33 can have directly opposing effects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study (Hung et al., 2020) showing context-dependent IL-33 effects.

claims.claim: HpARI2 binds strongly to the extracellular matrix and is retained in the local milieu of the parasite where it blocks IL-33 released in response to infection.
claims.source: In the context of the findings outlined here, we propose the following model for the HpARI family's effects: HpARI2 binds strongly to the extracellular matrix, and is retained in the local milieu of the parasite where it blocks IL-33 released in response to infection.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing HpARI2's HS binding and long half-life.

claims.claim: HpARI1 binds less strongly to HS and may diffuse slightly further from the site of deposition to block more distant IL-33 responses.
claims.source: HpARI1 binds less strongly to HS, and therefore may diffuse slightly further from the site of deposition, to block more distant IL-33 responses.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on HpARI1's weaker HS binding affinity.

claims.claim: HpARI3 lacks HS binding and diffuses freely to amplify IL-33 responses at distal sites, potentially amplifying IL-33-dependent regulatory responses.
claims.source: Finally, HpARI3 lacks HS binding and so diffuses freely to amplify IL-33 responses at distal sites, which we hypothesise could amplify IL-33-dependent regulatory responses.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on HpARI3's lack of HS binding and its IL-33-amplifying activity.

claims.claim: Transgenic parasites deficient for individual HpARI proteins would be useful to investigate the proposed model but have proved intractable for parasitic nematodes.
claims.source: To investigate these hypotheses, transgenic parasites deficient for individual HpARI proteins would be useful, however this has proved intractable for parasitic nematodes (Quinzo et al., 2022), and has not been achieved in H. polygyrus bakeri to date.
claims.evidence: Supported by cited study (Quinzo et al., 2022) about difficulties in nematode transgenesis.

claims.claim: Other parasitic helminths may have used extracellular matrix binding as a technique to retain immunoregulators within the local milieu.
claims.source: The findings outlined here may be applicable beyond H. polygyrus bakeri, as it appears likely that other parasitic helminths have used extracellular matrix binding as a technique to retain immunoregulators within the local milieu.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the findings with HpARI proteins.

claims.claim: Trichuris muris secretes the immunoregulatory protein p43 which binds and blocks IL-13 and has HS-binding activity.
claims.source: Indeed, Trichuris muris, another intestinal nematode, secretes the immunoregulatory protein p43. This protein binds and blocks IL-13, but also has HS-binding activity which has been proposed to tether p43 to the extracellular matrix, increasing survival of the protein at the site of infection (Bancroft et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by cited study (Bancroft et al., 2019).

claims.claim: H. polygyrus bakeri has developed a series of immunomodulatory protein families, including 10 Hp-TGMs and 2 HpBARIs.
claims.source: H. polygyrus bakeri has developed a series of immunomodulatory protein families, including 10 Hp-TGMs and 2 HpBARIs, therefore it will be informative to investigate whether members of these families also bind to the extracellular matrix, and whether this alters their in vivo localisation and/or half-life.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about H. polygyrus bakeri's immunomodulatory proteins.

claims.claim: A novel HS-binding ability of members of the HpARI family increases their in vivo half-life and activity at the site of deposition.
claims.source: In conclusion, we describe a novel HS-binding ability of members of the HpARI family and show that this binding increases their in vivo half-life and activity at the site of deposition.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

results.result: HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind DNA while HpARI3 does not, with HpARI1 showing reduced DNA-binding ability (50% binding) compared to HpARI2. HpARI2 suppresses IL-33 release via DNA tethering, while HpARI1 shows a non-significant trend and HpARI3 lacks this ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C40-C43 are supported by EMSA experiments (Figure 1D-E) and western blot analysis (Figure 1C). The differential DNA-binding abilities are clearly demonstrated with quantification showing HpARI1 binds only 50% of DNA. The IL-33 tethering function correlates with DNA binding, though HpARI1's effect did not reach statistical significance in the experiment shown.

results.result: DNA-binding ability is localized to the CCP1 domain and can be transferred through domain-swapped chimeras between HpARI2 and HpARI3. HpARI3:2 (with HpARI3 CCP1) lacks DNA binding while HpARI2:3 (with HpARI2 CCP1) shows DNA binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C44, C45, C47 are well-supported by domain-swap experiments shown in Figure 1F-G. The EMSA data clearly demonstrate that DNA binding follows the source of the CCP1 domain, providing strong evidence that this domain is both necessary and sufficient for DNA binding.

results.result: IL-33 tethering does not correlate with suppression of IL-33-induced responses at 24 hours. HpARI2:3 amplifies IL-33 responses despite tethering IL-33, while HpARI3:2 suppresses responses despite lacking tethering ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by comparing IL-33 tethering at 15 min (Figure 2B) with downstream responses at 24 hr (Figure 2D-H). This unexpected finding challenges the DNA tethering model and is a critical observation that led to the investigation of alternative mechanisms (HS binding). The data are internally consistent and statistically significant.

results.result: HpARI2 retains suppressive activity when administered 3 days prior to allergen, while HpARI3:2 only suppresses when administered 24 hr prior. The in vivo half-life is controlled by the CCP1 domain, with HpARI3 CCP1 conferring shorter half-life than HpARI2 CCP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 are supported by time-course experiments in Figure 3B-E showing differential persistence of activity. The data demonstrate that HpARI2 maintains activity at day -3 while HpARI3:2 loses activity, directly supporting the conclusion that CCP1 domain controls in vivo half-life. Statistical significance is shown for multiple readouts.

results.result: HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind to heparan sulphate (HS) while HpARI3 does not. This is demonstrated by gel filtration, heparin-agarose pull-down, and cell binding assays showing HpARI1/2 bind to CD45-negative stromal cells but HpARI3 does not bind any lung cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C11, C68-C71, C73-C75 are supported by multiple orthogonal binding assays (Figure 4A-C). The gel filtration shows differential elution, pull-down assays show selective binding, and cell-binding assays demonstrate interaction with stromal cells. The convergence of multiple independent methods provides strong support.

results.result: HpARI1 has an affinity for HS of 9.6 μM, HpARI2 has an affinity of 4.2 μM, and no binding could be detected between HpARI3 and HS by isothermal calorimetry.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 are supported by isothermal calorimetry experiments (Figure 4D-F) that provide quantitative binding affinities. The Kd values are clearly reported with stoichiometry (N) values near 1, indicating specific binding. The lack of binding for HpARI3 is also clearly demonstrated.

results.result: HpARI1 and HpARI2 contain a strongly positively charged surface in their CCP1 domains formed by five arginine residues, which acts as a non-specific binding site for negatively charged molecules including DNA and HS. HpARI3 lacks this charged surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C13, C79-C83 are supported by AlphaFold2 structural modeling and electrostatic surface analysis (Figure 5A) combined with molecular docking experiments (Figure 5B-C). The structural predictions are consistent with the experimental binding data. However, these are computational predictions rather than experimentally determined structures, which introduces some uncertainty.

results.result: A pentaR mutant of HpARI2 lacking five arginine residues retains IL-33 suppressive activity but loses DNA and HS binding, and has a shorter in vivo half-life than wild-type HpARI2. This demonstrates that the positively charged patch lengthens half-life via binding to DNA and HS.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87, C92 are supported by experiments with the HpARI2_pentaR mutant (Figure 6). The mutant shows identical IL-33 binding (Figure 6A) but lacks DNA/HS binding (Figure 6B-C) and has reduced in vivo activity at day -3 (Figure 6D-H). This structure-function analysis provides strong causal evidence linking the charged patch to half-life extension.

results.result: Extracellular matrix binding through HS interactions extends the in vivo half-life of HpARI2 at the site of administration, representing a novel mechanism for controlling protein persistence.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C88, C89, C114 represent the main conclusion supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: HS binding assays (Figure 4), domain-swap experiments (Figure 3), and pentaR mutant analysis (Figure 6). The data consistently show that HS binding correlates with extended half-life.

results.result: HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins retain the IL-33 modulation activities of their CCP2/3 domains, with small alterations in potency when CCP1 domains are swapped (HpARI2:3 EC50=21.5 ng/ml vs HpARI3 EC50=1.2 ng/ml; HpARI3:2 IC50=1.1 ng/ml vs HpARI2 IC50=1.9 ng/ml).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by in vitro ILC2 assays (Figure 2A) showing dose-response curves with calculated EC50/IC50 values. The fusion proteins retain their expected activities based on CCP2/3 domains, with modest changes in potency. The data are quantitative and reproducible across three biological replicates.

results.result: HpARI2 and HpARI2:3 tether IL-33 and reduce its release when co-administered with Alternaria, while HpARI3 and HpARI3:2 slightly increase IL-33 levels in BAL, possibly due to stabilization of soluble cytokine.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by western blot analysis (Figure 2B) showing differential IL-33 levels at 15 min. The tethering by HpARI2/HpARI2:3 is consistent with DNA binding, while the slight increase with HpARI3/HpARI3:2 is speculative but reasonable given their IL-33 binding without DNA tethering.

results.result: HpARI1 has lower affinity for DNA and HS compared to HpARI2, binding only 50% of DNA in EMSA assays. This may allow HpARI1 to remain partially in solution and diffuse further from the site of deposition.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by EMSA (Figure 1E) and ITC data (Figure 4D-E) showing weaker binding. However, claim C103 about functional significance is purely speculative without experimental evidence of differential diffusion or spatial activity patterns. The hypothesis is reasonable but untested.

results.result: The authors propose a model where HpARI1/2 have long-lasting effects due to HS/DNA binding that prevents diffusion and maintains local concentration, while HpARI3 lacks these interactions and diffuses freely to amplify IL-33 responses at distal sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C16, C91, C93, C107-C109 represent a proposed mechanistic model based on the experimental data. While the model is consistent with the observations (HS binding correlates with half-life), direct evidence for spatial localization, prevention of diffusion, or distal effects is lacking. The model is plausible but requires further validation, particularly regarding HpARI3's proposed role in amplifying distal regulatory responses.

results.result: Background claims establishing that H. polygyrus bakeri secretes the HpARI family of CCP domain proteins that bind IL-33 with opposing effects (HpARI1/2 suppress, HpARI3 amplifies), and that IL-33 is a pleiotropic cytokine with context-dependent pro-allergic or anti-inflammatory activities.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C17-C37 are background information supported by previous publications (Osbourn et al., 2017; Jamwal et al., 2023; Colomb et al., 2024) and established knowledge about IL-33 biology. These provide essential context for the current work and are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: HpARI2 dose-dependently suppresses ILC2 responses in vitro while HpARI3 amplifies them, as measured by IL-5 production.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by in vitro ILC2 assays (Figure 2A) and previous work (Colomb et al., 2024). The dose-response curves clearly show opposing effects with appropriate controls and replication.

results.result: The authors hypothesized that altered activity of fusion proteins could be due to their effective half-life in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 represents a hypothesis that was subsequently tested and supported by experiments in Figure 3. This hypothesis-driven approach led to the key findings about CCP1 domain control of half-life.

results.result: Background claims about extracellular DNA levels, HS localization, and precedent for CCP domain protein interactions with HS.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67, C72 are supported by cited literature (Curren et al., 2023; Mark et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2008; Xu and Esko, 2014) and provide rationale for investigating HS binding by HpARI proteins.

results.result: Discussion claims comparing HpARI2 to therapeutic antibodies, citing precedent for HS binding by cytokines and therapeutic proteins, and speculating about broader applicability to other helminth immunomodulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C94, C95-C101, C111-C113 are discussion points that place the findings in broader context. Claims C95-C98, C100, C112 are supported by cited literature. However, claims C94, C99, C111 are speculative comparisons or extrapolations without direct experimental support. These are reasonable interpretations but represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated facts.

results.result: Discussion claims about evolutionary selection of Hp-TGM proteins, context-dependent IL-33 effects in parasitic infection, and technical limitations of nematode transgenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C104-C106, C110 are supported by cited literature and provide context for interpreting the HpARI family's diverse functions. These are well-established concepts in the field.

results.result: HpARI1 can bind DNA but with reduced affinity compared to HpARI2 (binding only 50% of DNA in EMSA assays), while HpARI3 cannot bind DNA at all, as demonstrated by EMSA experiments.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers acknowledge the differential DNA-binding abilities of HpARI family members. The first reviewer states the data are 'convincing,' the second reviewer explicitly notes the authors 'identify two members of the family that bind via this domain,' and the third reviewer confirms the study 'builds upon their previous observation that HpARI2 binds DNA via its CCP1 domain.' No concerns are raised about these DNA-binding findings.

results.result: DNA-binding ability can be transferred through CCP1 domain-swapped chimeras between HpARI2 and HpARI3, with fusion proteins showing DNA binding directly related to the source of their CCP1 domain, demonstrating that DNA binding is mediated solely by the CCP1 domain.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept the domain-swap experiments without critique. The second reviewer explicitly states the authors 'identify two members of the family that bind via this domain in a non-specific manner,' implicitly accepting the domain-swap data that localizes binding to CCP1. No methodological concerns are raised about these chimeric protein experiments.

results.result: HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind to heparan sulphate (HS) with affinities of 9.6 μM and 4.2 μM respectively, while HpARI3 does not bind HS, as demonstrated by gel filtration, heparin-agarose pull-down, cell binding assays, and isothermal calorimetry.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept the heparan sulfate binding findings. The first reviewer describes the data as 'convincing,' the second reviewer explicitly states the authors 'identify two members of the family that bind...to the extracellular matrix molecule heparan sulphate,' and the third reviewer confirms 'the authors tested the CCP1 domain of HpARIs in binding heparan sulfate...and found that 1/2 bind heparan, but 3 cannot.' No concerns are raised about the multiple orthogonal binding assays.

results.result: HpARI1 and HpARI2 contain a strongly positively charged surface in their CCP1 domains formed by five arginine residues that acts as a non-specific binding site for negatively charged cellular components including DNA and HS, while HpARI3 lacks this charged surface.
results.evaluation: The structural modeling and electrostatic analysis are accepted by reviewers. The second reviewer explicitly notes the authors identify proteins that bind 'through a basic charged patch in CCP1,' directly referencing this structural finding. The first reviewer's statement that the data are 'convincing' encompasses these structural predictions. No concerns are raised about the AlphaFold modeling or docking experiments.

results.result: DNA-binding ability correlates with in vivo half-life of HpARI proteins, with HpARI2 suppressing allergen-induced responses when administered 3 days prior to allergen, while HpARI3:2 (containing HpARI3 CCP1) can only suppress when administered 24 hours prior, demonstrating that the CCP1 domain controls in vivo half-life.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept the half-life findings. The third reviewer explicitly states the study found that HS binding 'is related to their half-lives in vivo,' directly acknowledging this key result. The second reviewer notes the authors 'propose that binding to DNA or heparan sulphate extends the suppressive action,' accepting the correlation between binding and half-life. No concerns are raised about the time-course experiments.

results.result: A mutant of HpARI2 (HpARI2_pentaR) lacking five arginine residues has identical IL-33 suppressive activity in vitro but lacks binding to both heparin and DNA, and has a shorter in vivo half-life than wild-type HpARI2.
results.evaluation: The pentaR mutant experiments are accepted without critique. The reviewers' general acceptance of the manuscript's conclusions about HS binding controlling half-life implicitly includes acceptance of this key validation experiment. The first reviewer's statement that the data are 'convincing' and the comprehensive nature of the approaches noted by all reviewers encompasses these mutant studies.

results.result: Extracellular matrix binding through heparan sulphate extends the half-life of HpARI2 in vivo at the site of administration, representing a novel mechanism that increases the in vivo half-life and activity of HpARI family members at the site of deposition.
results.evaluation: This central conclusion is explicitly supported by all reviewers. The first reviewer calls this an 'important study' with 'convincing' data. The second reviewer states the authors 'propose that binding to DNA or heparan sulphate extends the suppressive action of these two parasite molecules.' The third reviewer confirms the study found HS binding 'is related to their half-lives in vivo.' This represents the main finding of the paper and is fully accepted.

results.result: IL-33 tethering does not correlate with suppression of IL-33-induced responses at 24 hours, as HpARI2:3 amplifies responses despite tethering IL-33, and HpARI3:2 effectively blocks responses despite lacking tethering, indicating the DNA tethering model cannot fully explain protein activity.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept this unexpected finding that challenges the simple tethering model. The second reviewer acknowledges the authors' proposal that the third family member 'has a shorter half-life and may function via diffusion,' implicitly accepting the data showing tethering alone is insufficient. No concerns are raised about these counterintuitive results that led to the HS binding hypothesis.

results.result: HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins retain the amplifying or suppressing activities of their CCP2/3 domains, with small alterations in potency (HpARI2:3 EC50=21.5 ng/ml vs HpARI3 EC50=1.2 ng/ml; HpARI3:2 IC50=1.1 ng/ml vs HpARI2 IC50=1.9 ng/ml).
results.evaluation: The functional characterization of fusion proteins is accepted without critique. The reviewers' acceptance of the overall conclusions about differential activities of family members implicitly includes acceptance of these in vitro functional data. The first reviewer notes the 'comprehensive approaches' used, which would include these dose-response experiments.

results.result: HpARI2 suppresses IL-33 release measured by western blot due to tethering, HpARI1 shows a non-significant trend toward suppression, HpARI3 does not alter IL-33 release, and fusion proteins show tethering patterns consistent with their CCP1 domains.
results.evaluation: The IL-33 tethering data are accepted as part of the overall characterization. The second reviewer explicitly acknowledges the authors' work 'extends previous studies by this group showing the binding of DNA by members of this family,' which includes the tethering mechanism. No concerns are raised about the western blot quantification or interpretation.

results.result: HpARI2 dose-dependently suppresses ILC2 responses in vitro while HpARI3 amplifies them, as demonstrated in IL-33-stimulated ILC2 assays.
results.evaluation: The differential activities of HpARI2 and HpARI3 are fully accepted. The second reviewer explicitly states the family members exhibit 'differential activities, either suppressive or enhancing,' directly acknowledging these in vitro functional data. The first reviewer's statement about 'comprehensive approaches' encompasses these functional assays.

results.result: The authors propose a model where suppressive HpARI1 and HpARI2 have long-lasting effects due to DNA/HS interactions that prevent diffusion and maintain local concentration, while HpARI3 has a shorter half-life and diffuses freely to amplify IL-33 responses at distal sites.
results.evaluation: The proposed model is accepted by reviewers. The second reviewer explicitly states 'the authors thus propose that binding to DNA or heparan sulphate extends the suppressive action of these two parasite molecules, whereas the third family member does not bind and consequently has a shorter half-life and may function via diffusion,' directly endorsing the model. The first reviewer's assessment that the paper is 'important' and 'relevant' indicates acceptance of the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: HpARI1 has lower affinity for DNA and HS compared to HpARI2, and may remain partially in solution to diffuse further from the site of deposition and mediate effects at greater distances.
results.evaluation: The differential binding affinities and their functional implications are accepted. The reviewers' acceptance of the overall model of differential localization based on binding affinities implicitly includes acceptance of HpARI1's intermediate properties. No concerns are raised about this aspect of the model.

results.result: H. polygyrus bakeri secretes the HpARI family of three CCP domain-containing proteins that bind IL-33, with HpARI1 and HpARI2 suppressing responses while HpARI3 enhances responses by stabilizing the cytokine, representing structurally similar molecules with opposing physiological effects.
results.evaluation: This background information is fully accepted by all reviewers. The second reviewer explicitly describes 'the family of HpARI proteins binds to the alarmin interleukin 33 and depending on family members, exhibits differential activities, either suppressive or enhancing.' The third reviewer confirms 'HpARI1/2 has suppressive functions, while HpARI3 can enhance the interaction between IL-33 and its receptor.' This represents established context from prior work.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the differential DNA-binding abilities of HpARI family members (C6, C7, C43). OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of EMSA and western blot data, while peer reviewers describe findings as 'convincing' without methodological concerns. OpenEval also addresses additional claims (C40, C41, C42) about IL-33 tethering that peer reviewers group separately.

Both evaluations support the domain-swap experiments demonstrating CCP1 domain control of DNA binding (C8, C45, C47). OpenEval explicitly describes the EMSA evidence as 'strong,' while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings without critique. OpenEval addresses C44 which is not explicitly mentioned in peer review.

Perfect agreement on claims C56-C59 regarding the unexpected finding that DNA tethering alone doesn't predict long-term activity. Both recognize this as a critical observation that challenged the simple tethering model and led to investigation of HS binding. OpenEval emphasizes statistical significance while peer reviewers accept the counterintuitive nature of the results.

Both evaluations support the time-course experiments showing CCP1 domain control of in vivo half-life (C61-C64). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of statistical significance across multiple readouts. Peer reviewers accept the correlation between binding and half-life, with R5 also including C9 which OpenEval doesn't explicitly group with these claims.

Strong agreement on heparan sulfate binding findings (C10, C11, C68-C71, C73-C75). OpenEval emphasizes the convergence of multiple orthogonal methods (gel filtration, pull-down, cell-binding assays). Peer reviewers describe data as 'convincing' and explicitly acknowledge the identification of HS-binding family members. Peer R3 also includes ITC data (C76-C78) which OpenEval addresses separately.

Both support the quantitative binding affinity data from ITC experiments (C76-C78). OpenEval provides technical assessment of Kd values and stoichiometry. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the broader HS binding characterization without raising concerns. Peer R3 groups these with other HS binding assays while OpenEval treats them separately.

Perfect agreement on structural modeling and electrostatic analysis (C12, C13, C79-C83). OpenEval notes these are computational predictions rather than experimental structures, introducing some uncertainty. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the identification of the 'basic charged patch in CCP1' and accept the AlphaFold modeling without concerns.

Both support the pentaR mutant validation experiments (C84-C87). OpenEval emphasizes this as strong causal evidence linking the charged patch to half-life extension and includes C92. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of the overall HS binding mechanism. Peer R6 also includes C14 which OpenEval doesn't group here.

Perfect agreement on the main conclusion that HS binding controls half-life extension (C39, C88, C89, C114). OpenEval emphasizes convergence of multiple lines of evidence. All peer reviewers explicitly endorse this central finding, with the first calling it 'important' and 'convincing,' and the third confirming HS binding 'is related to their half-lives in vivo.'

Perfect agreement on in vitro ILC2 functional assays (C51-C53). OpenEval provides technical assessment of dose-response curves and EC50/IC50 values with quantitative reproducibility. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of 'comprehensive approaches' without raising methodological concerns.

Both support the IL-33 tethering data (C54-C55). OpenEval notes the speculation about HpARI3/HpARI3:2 effects. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the DNA binding characterization. Peer R10 also includes C40-C42 which OpenEval groups with R1.

Perfect agreement on claims C102-C103 regarding HpARI1's intermediate binding properties. However, evaluations differ in confidence: OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting C103 about functional significance is 'purely speculative without experimental evidence.' Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the differential binding and localization model without expressing concerns about speculation.

Perfect agreement on claims C15, C16, C91, C93, C107-C109 regarding the mechanistic model. However, evaluations differ in confidence: OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting 'direct evidence for spatial localization, prevention of diffusion, or distal effects is lacking.' Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, with the second reviewer explicitly endorsing the proposed model including diffusion-based function of the third family member.

Both support the background information and established context (C1-C4, C25, C34-C37). OpenEval references prior publications and established IL-33 biology. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the HpARI family's differential activities and prior work. OpenEval addresses many additional background claims (C17-C24, C26-C33) not explicitly mentioned in peer review.

Perfect agreement on the differential activities of HpARI2 and HpARI3 in vitro (C49-C50). OpenEval references prior work and dose-response curves. Peer reviewers explicitly state family members exhibit 'differential activities, either suppressive or enhancing' and accept these functional data as part of comprehensive approaches.
